fact_text: The guest said the cost of generating electricity makes up about 45 to 50 percent of a Pakistani power bill, split into capacity payments and energy cost.

fact_text: The guest put Pakistan's generation cost at about Rs24 per unit: roughly Rs14 to 15 of capacity payment plus about Rs9 of energy (fuel) cost.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: The guest said Indian generators produce power for about Rs12 to 13 per unit, with energy cost near Rs3 and capacity payments near Rs8, which lets them sell at about Rs26 to 28.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: The guest said Pakistan sells residential power at about Rs56 per unit and commercial at about Rs75, far above the roughly Rs24 cost of generating it.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: The guest said about 70 percent of India's power output runs on domestic coal, which he put at about Rs4.5 per unit of fuel cost.

fact_text: The guest cited a 2006 survey putting Pakistan's Thar coal reserves at about 175 billion tonnes, and said Thar lignite needs about 800 kg of coal per megawatt-hour.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: The guest said the 2015 energy policy added about 10,000 MW of new capacity: 5,000 MW of LNG and 5,000 MW of coal, of which about 4,000 MW used technology unable to burn Thar lignite.

fact_text: The guest cited a 2005 World Bank report saying Pakistan's foreign-exchange capacity could fund only about 2,000 to 3,000 MW of power running on imported fuel.

fact_text: The guest said the imported-fuel agreements charge for about 70 percent of plant capacity, against roughly 30 percent under the earlier World Bank-based plan, so consumers carry the extra roughly 40 percent.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: In the guest's Rs60 bill example, production cost is Rs24 (about Rs9 fuel and Rs14 to 15 capacity), and the rest of the bill goes to line losses, distribution and debt repayment.

fact_text: The guest said Pakistan borrowed about Rs1 trillion from the market to clear power circular debt, and consumers pay about Rs3 per unit to service it.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: The guest said the interest on that power circular-debt borrowing alone is roughly equal to Punjab's annual development programme.
source_name: Nukta Business, 'Why Is Electricity Expensive in Pakistan? | Truth About IPPs, Solar & Load Shedding | Nukta Business' (YouTube, 2026-07-28)

fact_text: As of 2026-07-28 the guest said LNG-based generation costs about Rs40 per unit, versus about Rs25 for Thar coal-based generation.

fact_text: Pakistan's long-term LNG contracts, including one with Qatar, are take-or-pay, so the fuel must be paid for even when it is not used, which forces costly generation.

fact_text: The guest hoped the government would renegotiate LNG contract terms around 2026, about ten years after the 2015 contracts were signed.

fact_text: The guest said Indian coal plants source coal domestically and are not exposed to Strait of Hormuz disruptions, unlike Pakistan's LNG-dependent plants.

fact_text: The guest said grid electricity demand is flat or falling as consumers shift to solar, even though total electricity demand is still growing.

fact_text: The guest said about 80 percent of rural tubewells in Pakistan had been solarised as of 2026-07-28.

fact_text: The guest said net metering was introduced in 2014 but only took off around 2018-19, when rising power tariffs pushed households to install solar.

fact_text: The guest cited an NGO estimate that about 500 MW of solar panels were imported and about 400 MW installed, and said about 10,000 MW of panels are imported each year.

fact_text: The guest described older net metering as a one-for-one credit, newer gross metering as selling surplus at one price while buying at the full market rate, and hybrid systems as battery-stored solar sold back at peak.

fact_text: Solar output peaks roughly 8am to 3pm, so the guest said hybrid users charge batteries in that window and draw on them after sunset.

fact_text: The guest cited Lucky Cement as an industrial user that added a battery system so it can use its own solar power as much as possible.

fact_text: The guest said self-generation with a battery and meter costs about Rs30 to 35 per unit, against about Rs65 per unit bought from the utility.

fact_text: The guest said about 55 to 60 percent of Islamabad households rent, about 40 percent in Karachi and 30 to 35 percent in Lahore, and renters cannot take solar panels with them when they move.

fact_text: The guest said about 95 percent of rural residents own their homes or land, which makes rooftop and ground solar easier to install there.

fact_text: The guest argued that households leaving the grid shift the grid's fixed costs onto poorer and non-solar consumers, who cannot afford solar.

fact_text: The guest warned that if large numbers of users leave the grid, demand will fall further and the remaining customers will face higher per-unit charges.

fact_text: The guest said the 200-unit subsidy may be restricted to registered households through a QR-code system, so only eligible users receive it.

fact_text: The guest said the gap between about Rs24 generation cost and a Rs56 sale price is about Rs30 per unit, which across consumption he estimated at about 12.5 billion dollars a year, about 2.5 percent of GDP.

fact_text: The guest said rooftop solar exporting onto a feeder causes reverse power flow, which requires smart grid monitoring and protection changes at substations and feeders.
